query: Earlier refractory high-entropy alloys illustrate persistent trade-offs: MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW retained good yield strength from 600 to 1600 °C, with MoNbTaVW reaching 842 MPa at 1000 °C, but both had poor room-temperature fracture toughness and high density; HfNbTaTiZr showed room-temperature ductility above 50% and a yield strength of 929 MPa but only 295 MPa at 1000 °C; and as-cast HfMoTaTiZr achieved about 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at elevated temperature but retained a density of 10.21 g cm−3. Given the constraint that density must be reduced without sacrificing the strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, what single intervention should be tested? Provide a mechanistic hypothesis, predicted outcomes relative to the as-cast baseline, explicit temperature and loading boundary conditions, supporting evidence from the preceding RHEA results, and a controlled experiment with quantitative rejection criteria that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partial substitution of some heavy Hf atoms with a lightweight refractory element (e.g., Al) will reduce the overall density of as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr while maintaining its high room‐temperature and high‐temperature yield strengths by preserving the solid-solution strengthening effect through severe lattice distortion.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy with a density of about 10.21 g/cm³, a room-temperature yield strength of approximately 1600 MPa, and an elevated-temperature (around 1000 °C) yield strength of roughly 855 MPa.
generation.intervention: Replace a controlled fraction of Hf with aluminum to form an alloy analogous to HfAlMoTaTiZr via conventional casting methods.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests under compressive loading at room temperature and at the specified high temperature using a standard strain rate as employed in prior RHEA studies.
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of a single-phase body-centered cubic solid solution with maintained lattice distortion that facilitates solid-solution strengthening without forming secondary phases.
generation.mechanism: By partially substituting heavy Hf with lightweight Al, the average atomic weight is reduced while severe lattice distortion is preserved, thereby maintaining the solid-solution strengthening mechanism and ensuring comparable yield strengths.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is expected to achieve a density reduction on the order of approximately 10–15% relative to 10.21 g/cm³ while retaining yield strengths close to (at least >90% of) the original values of ~1600 MPa at room temperature and ~855 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with high density (10.21 g/cm³) and high yield strengths at room (≈1600 MPa) and elevated (≈855 MPa at 1000 °C) temperatures.
generation.boundary: Compressive mechanical performance must be evaluated under test conditions at room temperature and at 1000 °C with strain rates comparable to previous studies (e.g., ~10⁻³ s⁻¹). The alloy must retain at least 90% of the original yield strengths while showing a density reduction of at least 10%.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal level of Hf substitution and any potential impacts on ductility, fracture toughness, or phase stability remain uncertain and will need to be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of alloys with varying levels of Hf-to-Al substitution (e.g., Hf₁₋ₓAlₓMoTaTiZr with x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75) using the same casting method. Perform density measurements, and compressive tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C (strain rate ~10⁻³ s⁻¹). Conduct XRD and microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM) to confirm phase stability and single-phase BCC structure.
measurements: Phase identification from XRD and microstructure observations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with 50% Hf substitution (or the composition nearest the predicted optimum) does not exhibit at least a 10% reduction in density while retaining at least 90% of the baseline yield strengths at both room temperature and 1000 °C, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Adding lightweight elements into RHEAs can effectively reduce the density and improve the specific strength [,,,]. For example, Senkov et al. fabricated Al0.4Hf0.6NbTaTiZr RHEA by adding Al into the HfNbTaTiZr RHEA. The density of the alloy decreased from 9.94 to 9.05 g/cm3, and the specific yield strength increased from 93.56 to 203.43 MPa∙cm3/g []. However, their plasticity deteriorated significantly. Recently, Yang et al. found that NbTiVTaAl0.25 RHEA with Al addition still have outstanding compressive plasticity greater than 50% []. Nevertheless, the specific strength of this alloy is only 151.48 MPa∙cm3/g, which has the potential for further improvement. In this work, a series of lightweight TaNbVTi-based RHEAs were fabricated by mechanical alloying (MA) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS). The microstructural evolution and its effects on mechanical properties were analyzed.
